title: Principal Component Analysis
body:
**PCA finds the directions your data actually varies in, and lets you throw away the rest.** It is
the destination of the whole first half of this course, and the vault's only route from the MATH
block into [[MACHINE LEARNING]]: the chain runs [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] →
[[Spectral Theorem]] → [[Singular Value Decomposition]] → here.

The problem it solves: data with $p$ features lives in $\mathbb{R}^p$, which is unplottable past
three and full of near-duplicate features that carry the same information twice. PCA replaces the
$p$ original axes with $k \ll p$ new ones, chosen so that projecting onto them loses as little as
possible.

## The convention, first

> **The data matrix $X$ is $n \times p$: one row per sample, one column per feature.**
> This is the one place the vault stores data along rows rather than columns. Vectors are still
> columns everywhere else ([[Matrix Multiplication]], $A\mathbf{x}$); a *sample* is a row of $X$
> because that is how every dataset, spreadsheet, and dataframe is written.

Getting this backwards is the classic PCA error, and it is not cosmetic. With samples as rows the
covariance matrix is $X_c^TX_c$ ($p \times p$, feature by feature) and the principal directions
are the **right** singular vectors, the columns of $V$. Transpose the convention and it becomes
$X_cX_c^T$ and the **left** singular vectors instead. Write the convention at the top of any
derivation before you write anything else.

## The algorithm

1. **Centre.** Subtract each column's mean: $X_c = X - \mathbf{1}\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T$. Not optional.
   Skip it and the first component points at the mean rather than at the variation, because
   variance is defined about the mean.
2. **Covariance.** $C = \frac{1}{n-1}X_c^TX_c$, a $p \times p$ symmetric positive semidefinite
   matrix. Its diagonal holds the feature variances and its off-diagonal the covariances.
3. **Decompose.** $C$ is symmetric, so the [[Spectral Theorem]] gives $C = QDQ^T$ with real
   eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. The eigenvectors are the **principal components** and
   the eigenvalues are the variance along each.
4. **Order and truncate.** Sort by $\lambda$ descending, keep the top $k$ columns of $Q$ as $Q_k$.
5. **Project.** $Z = X_cQ_k$, an $n \times k$ matrix of scores. This is a [[Projection]] onto the
   subspace spanned by the top $k$ components, and it is the reduced dataset.

In practice you do not form $C$ at all. Take the SVD of $X_c$ directly: $X_c = U\Sigma V^T$ gives
$V = Q$ and $\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2/(n-1)$, with better conditioning, since forming $X_c^TX_c$
squares the condition number the way it does in [[Least Squares]]. **Library PCA is a truncated
SVD.**

## Why the top eigenvector is the right answer

Variance along a unit direction $\mathbf{w}$ is

$$
\text{Var}(X_c\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^TC\mathbf{w}
$$

a [[Quadratic Form]]. Maximising it subject to $\|\mathbf{w}\| = 1$ is a constrained optimisation
whose answer, by the principal axes theorem, is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, with
maximum value $\lambda_1$. The second component maximises the same thing among directions
orthogonal to the first, and so on. **So the components are uncorrelated by construction**, not
by luck: orthogonal eigenvectors of the covariance matrix means zero covariance in the new
coordinates, which is $C$ diagonalised.

The other reading is equivalent and sometimes more useful: the top $k$ components are the
subspace minimising total squared reconstruction error, by
[[Low-Rank Approximation|Eckart-Young-Mirsky]]. **Maximise the variance you keep and minimise the
error you make are the same optimisation**, because the two add up to the fixed total.

## Reading the output

- **Explained variance ratio** $\lambda_i / \sum_j \lambda_j$: the share of total variance on
  component $i$. Plotting these is the **scree plot**, and $k$ is chosen at the elbow or by a
  cumulative threshold such as 95%.
- **Loadings**: the entries of each eigenvector, saying which original features it is built from.
  This is how a component gets interpreted, and it is also PCA's main weakness: a component is a
  combination of everything and rarely means anything you can name.
- **Reconstruction**: $\hat{X}_c = ZQ_k^T$, back in the original $p$ coordinates but confined to
  the $k$-dimensional subspace.

## Cautions

- **Scale matters.** Covariance is not scale invariant, so a feature measured in millimetres will
  dominate one measured in metres. Standardise to unit variance first, which is the same as
  running PCA on the correlation matrix rather than the covariance matrix.
- **PCA is linear.** It finds a flat subspace. Data on a curved manifold (a spiral, a sphere) is
  not helped, which is what [[Non-Linear|non-linear]] methods exist for.
- **Variance is not the same as usefulness.** The direction of most variance may be irrelevant to
  the label you are predicting. PCA is unsupervised and never looks at $y$.
- Components are determined up to sign, so two runs can differ by a flip and nothing is wrong.

## Where the degree uses it

Dimensionality reduction before [[Classification]], so a model trains on 20 features instead of
2000, and visualisation of high-dimensional data by projecting to $k = 2$. Eigenfaces are PCA on
face images, which is [[Computer Vision]]'s classical method and the point where this note meets
[[Image Processing]]. In [[MACHINE LEARNING]] it is the standard preprocessing step for the curse
of dimensionality, and it is what "dimensionality reduction" means unless something else is said.

## Related

- [[Spectral Theorem]], [[Singular Value Decomposition]], [[Low-Rank Approximation]]
- [[Projection]] and [[Quadratic Form]]: the two derivations
- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] and [[Diagonalization]] (MATH 1203): the prerequisite
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]], [[Image Processing]], [[NumPy]]
- [[CNN]] and [[Computer Vision]] (`Books/`): eigenfaces are the *linear* answer to the same
  question a convolutional network answers non-linearly, which is who designs the features
- [[Variance]] and [[Correlation]] ([[STATISTICS]], MATH 2234): the covariance matrix this note
  eigen-decomposes is built entirely out of those two definitions, "direction of greatest variance"
  is that quantity maximised over directions, and components being uncorrelated is
  orthogonality restated in statistical language
